say.text: Two patients in the bay, both in shock, both with absent breath sounds on the right.
Tension pneumothorax or massive haemothorax? Which finding tells them apart?

choices.label: Absent breath sounds on the injured side
Muffled heart sounds with a falling pressure
Hyper-resonance on percussion, with distended neck veins
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Both sides are silent, so silence cannot separate them. Which bedside signs does air change, and which does blood change?
Air trapped under pressure makes the chest hyper-resonant and fills the neck veins. Blood dulls the percussion note.
The veins are often flat in blood loss from hypovolaemia, so percussion and neck veins are the discriminators, not breath sounds.
Yes. Air gives a hyper-resonant chest and distended neck veins; blood gives dullness, and its neck veins are often flat.
That choice is not right. Both patients are silent on that side, so silence feels like the sign that settles it.
Massive haemothorax is also silent on one side, so silence cannot separate the two.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the shared sign: silence on one side fits both.

say.text: That choice is not right. A falling pressure with a full neck feels like a heart-level problem, so the heart sounds seem to decide it.
Muffled heart sounds belong to the pericardium, and they do not separate air from blood in the chest.

sure_note.text: You were sure: muffled heart sounds point to the pericardium, not the pleura.

say.text: A stab wound to the right chest. He is hypotensive, his neck veins are distended, the right chest is hyper-resonant and breath sounds on that side are absent.
What is your next step?

choices.label: Portable chest X-ray first, then decide on treatment
Immediate needle decompression of the right chest
Intubate and ventilate with positive pressure
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Count what is in front of you: low pressure, a full neck and a silent side. Which step cannot wait for a film?
A one-way valve traps air in the pleural space; it collapses the lung and impedes venous return.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, so decompress first, then tube and reassess, rather than wait for an X-ray.
Yes. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and immediate needle decompression comes before anything else.
That choice is not right. A film feels like the careful step before any procedure, and that habit is strong.
A film can wait only while the patient is stable, and this one is in shock.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the habit: imaging first is the trap in shock.

say.text: That choice is not right. Airway is the first letter, so a tube feels like the first move.
Positive pressure only adds air to a space that already has a one-way leak, so the chest is the problem first.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a secure airway does not treat the leak that is filling the chest.

say.text: Picture an untreated tension pneumothorax, with air already trapped by a one-way valve.
You now push positive-pressure breaths in. What happens to the pressure in that space?

choices.label: It pushes more air into the trapped space, raising pressure
It re-expands the collapsed lung and relieves the shift
It pulls the mediastinum toward the collapsed lung
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Air that enters the pleural space through the leak has no way out. Ask what another breath does to that trapped air.
The valve lets air in and not out, so pleural pressure rises with every breath.
Rising pressure shifts the mediastinum to the other side and impedes venous return, so it must be relieved first.
Yes. Trapped air under rising pressure pushes the mediastinum and cuts venous return.
That choice is not right. Re-inflating a collapsed lung is what a breath is meant to do, so the picture feels right.
Here the valve lets air in and not out. Ask what a breath does to a space the valve keeps filling.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a one-way leak fills the space; it does not drain it.

say.text: That choice is not right. A collapsed lung looks like it should drag things toward it, so the pull feels plausible.
Ask what is doing the pushing here: the collapsed lung, or the air under pressure.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the trapped air is pushing, not the lung pulling.

say.text: In the primary survey, what confirms a tension pneumothorax?

choices.label: Upright chest X-ray showing a shifted mediastinum
Bedside clinical findings on examination of the chest
CT chest before treatment, to see the pleura
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The primary survey runs on what kills in minutes. Which of these can be found at the bedside, without a machine?
The diagnosis is clinical: unilateral absent breath sounds, hyper-resonance, distended neck veins and shock.
The physiology kills while you wait, so the bedside signs decide the step, and imaging follows only once the patient is stable.
Yes. The diagnosis is clinical, and a film is not needed before treatment.
That choice is not right. A film is what most exam stems pair with a chest diagnosis, so the X-ray feels like the confirmation.
A film can wait only while the patient is stable. The primary survey runs on what kills in minutes, and a film takes longer.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a film is the habit, not the primary survey's test.

say.text: That choice is not right. CT is the thorough test in trauma, so it feels like the complete answer.
Thorough is not the same as first; the primary survey is built on what can be done at the bedside.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a thorough scan is not the first test in the primary survey.

say.text: ATLS 10th edition: where is needle decompression placed in an adult?

choices.label: 2nd intercostal space, in the mid-clavicular line
3rd intercostal space, at the anterior axillary line
4th or 5th intercostal space, anterior to the mid-axillary line
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Two editions give two answers. Which one is the current adult site, and why would chest wall thickness matter?
ATLS 10th edition places the adult site in the 4th or 5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.
A catheter at the old site can be too short to reach the pleura through a thick adult chest wall.
Yes. The adult site is the 4th or 5th space, anterior to the mid-axillary line, where a catheter can reach the pleura.
That choice is not right. It is the site most older books and past keys give, so it feels like the standard answer.
That site is the child's ATLS site, and the adult site has moved since, so the edition matters here.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so hold both keys: old and current editions differ on the adult site.

say.text: That choice is not right. It sits close to the right area, so a half-remembered site picks it up.
Near-misses lose the exact interspace and line that ATLS names, so check both the space and the line.

sure_note.text: You were sure, but the exact space and line are what the exam tests.

say.text: A 6-year-old has a tension pneumothorax with the same signs as an adult.
Where do you place the needle now?

choices.label: 4th or 5th space, just anterior to mid-axillary line
2nd intercostal space, at the mid-clavicular line
Chest X-ray to choose the site before needling
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The age in the stem matters. Which site does the child keep, and which did the adult edition change?
ATLS keeps the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line for children, while the adult site moved.
A child's thinner chest wall lets a short catheter still reach the pleura at that site.
Yes. In a child the site is the 2nd intercostal space at the mid-clavicular line; the adult site is for adults.
That choice is not right. You learned the current adult site most recently, so it is the one that comes to mind.
The adult site does not carry over to a child; ATLS keeps a different site by age.

sure_note.text: You were sure: the site follows age and edition, not the most recent memory.

say.text: That choice is not right. A film feels safe before any procedure, even in a child.
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis at any age, and a film does not choose the site.

sure_note.text: You were sure, so check the habit: imaging first is the trap in this condition.

say.text: On the right, the lung keeps collapsing and the trapped air keeps pushing.
Which way does the mediastinum move?

choices.label: It is pulled toward the collapsed right lung
It is pushed to the left, impeding venous return
It shifts right, toward the injured side with the lung
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask what is doing the pushing: the collapsed lung, or the air trapped under pressure? Then ask which way that push goes.
Rising pleural pressure pushes the mediastinum to the opposite side and impedes venous return.
So the trachea moves away from the injured side, and the neck veins fill.
Yes. Trapped air under rising pressure pushes the mediastinum across and impedes venous return.
That choice is not right. A collapsed lung looks like it should drag its neighbours in with it.
The force here is air under rising pressure, not the lung's pull.

sure_note.text: You were sure: pressure pushes, and the collapsed lung does not drag.

say.text: That choice is not right. Shifting toward the injured side is what a collapsed lung seems to do on a picture.
The direction is set by the pressure, not by the side of the injury. Check which way the trachea moves.

sure_note.text: You were sure: check the direction, because it is the detail the exam tests.

say.text: A right-sided tension pneumothorax, examined at the bedside.
Which pair of findings do you expect?

choices.label: Trachea deviated to the left, hyper-resonance on the right
Trachea deviated to the right, hyper-resonance on the right
Trachea central, with dullness to percussion on the right
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Think about where the pressure pushes the trachea, and which percussion note trapped air gives.
Trapped air under pressure pushes the trachea to the opposite side and leaves the injured chest hyper-resonant.
The same pressure impedes venous return, which is why the neck veins fill.
Yes. Hyper-resonance on the injured side, with the trachea pushed to the other side, is the expected pair.
That choice is not right. The trachea tracks the injured side in many pictures, so it feels like the same side.
Air pushes from the inside, so ask which way that push would move the trachea.
That choice is not right. Dullness is the sign of blood, so a dull right chest feels like it belongs to this picture.
Dullness and a central trachea describe a different chest, not this one.
A man has three ribs each broken in two places, and a segment of chest wall moves paradoxically. His saturation is falling.
What is the main cause of his hypoxia?

choices.label: Paradoxical movement of the flail segment
Underlying pulmonary contusion of the lung beneath
An associated open pneumothorax from the same injury
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The moving segment is what you can see. Ask what the lung under it is doing to the blood's oxygen.
A flail segment is two or more adjacent ribs, each fractured in two or more places.
The hypoxia comes from the contusion underneath; the paradoxical movement is only the visible sign.
Yes. The contusion causes the hypoxia; the paradoxical movement is only its sign.
That choice is not right. The moving segment is the visible injury, so it is easy to take for the cause.
The moving segment is a sign of the injury. Ask what the lung underneath is doing.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a sign you can see is not the same as the cause.

say.text: That choice is not right. Any chest injury on the list feels like a candidate for the hypoxia.
Being on the chest-injury list does not make a problem the cause here. Ask what flail chest does to the lung.

sure_note.text: You were sure: a listed injury is not automatically the cause.

say.text: Flail chest with a bruised lung on the monitor, and his saturation is still falling.
Which management treats the cause?

choices.label: Urgent surgical fixation of the loose segment
Strapping the chest wall to stop the movement
Oxygen, analgesia, judicious fluids, ventilation if needed
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: The question asks what treats the cause, the bruised lung, not the sign. Which options act on the lung?
Flail chest with pulmonary contusion is managed with oxygen, adequate analgesia, judicious fluids and ventilation if hypoxia persists.
The target is the lung, because the contusion is what causes the hypoxia.
Yes. Treat the contusion with oxygen, analgesia and judicious fluids, ventilating if hypoxia persists.
That choice is not right. A visibly broken chest feels like it needs a decisive fix, so surgery sounds right.
Fixing the segment treats the sign you can see; the hypoxia sits in the lung beneath it.
That choice is not right. Strapping feels like a gentle way to stop the movement that alarms you.
Stopping the movement does not address the contusion, which is what lowers the oxygen.
A stab wound left of the sternum. He is hypotensive, his neck veins are distended and his heart sounds are muffled.
Breath sounds are clear on both sides. What is the most likely diagnosis?

choices.label: Cardiac tamponade, with blood compressing the heart
Massive haemothorax, dull and silent on one side
Tension pneumothorax on the left, hyper-resonant
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Look at the sounds. Which findings here point at the heart rather than the pleura, and what do both lungs sound like?
Beck's triad is hypotension, muffled heart sounds and distended neck veins; it is the tamponade picture.
Clear breath sounds on both sides, and no one-sided dullness, separate it from the pleural causes.
Yes. Beck's triad with clear breath sounds on both sides points to the pericardium.
That choice is not right. Shock with a silent side feels like blood in the chest, so the haemothorax picture seems close.
Both sides are clear here, and haemothorax needs a dull, silent side.

sure_note.text: You were sure: check the breath sounds on each side before naming the pleura.

say.text: That choice is not right. Hypotension with full neck veins feels like the obstructive air picture.
Clear breath sounds on both sides argue against a pleural air leak.

sure_note.text: You were sure: an air leak is one-sided, and these breath sounds are not.

say.text: The primary survey lists the chest injuries that threaten life in minutes.
Which is NOT one of them?

choices.label: Massive haemothorax, with blood in the chest
Cardiac tamponade, with blood around the heart
Simple closed pneumothorax, with the lung still inflating
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Ask which of these would stop breathing or filling within minutes, and which injury is minor and can wait.
The five are tension pneumothorax, open pneumothorax, massive haemothorax, flail chest with pulmonary contusion and cardiac tamponade.
A simple closed pneumothorax is not on that list, so it is the one that is NOT.
Yes. Simple closed pneumothorax is not among the five; the other four are.
That choice is not right. Any big chest bleed feels like it belongs on a list of chest killers.
The list is built on what threatens breathing or filling, and massive haemothorax is on it.
That choice is not right. A heart problem can feel like a separate case, so it drops off the chest list.
Cardiac tamponade is one of the five and is assessed with circulation.
Chest injuries are sorted in the primary survey by the letter they threaten.
Which injury is assessed under circulation rather than breathing?

choices.label: Tension pneumothorax, under the breathing letter
Cardiac tamponade, under the circulation letter
Flail chest with pulmonary contusion, under breathing
Not sure, give me a hint

say.text: Tamponade fills the sac around the heart. Which letter of the primary survey covers the heart's filling?
Cardiac tamponade is the chest injury assessed with circulation, and Beck's triad is its picture.
Tension pneumothorax and flail chest are breathing problems, so they belong under B.
Yes. Cardiac tamponade is the injury assessed under circulation; the rest of the chest list is under breathing.
That choice is not right. A chest injury feels like a breathing problem, so the tension one comes to mind first.
Ask which chest injury stops the heart filling rather than the lung inflating.
That choice is not right. Flail chest is the classic breathing injury, so it sounds right under B.
Flail chest threatens breathing through the chest wall and lung, not the filling of the heart.
